title: Asking, answering, saying no
goal: Ask questions in two ways, say "not" with a single word, and discover that Swedish has two different words for "yes" that must never be mixed up.
bekal: make yes/no questions just by swapping two words
seven question words that cover almost everything you need at A1
put *inte* in the right place, and answer with *jo*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — I köket
dialogs.intro: The first evening. Dian opens the cupboard in the shared kitchen and finds a row of things she doesn't recognize. Ahmad, a housemate who has already spent a year in Stockholm, is sitting at the table.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Det är filmjölk. Det är inte mjölk.
lines.literal: it is film-milk. it is not milk.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ja, mycket gott. Man äter det till frukost.
lines.id: Yes, really good. People eat it for breakfast.
lines.literal: yes, very tasty. one eats it for breakfast.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Det är Oskar. Han bor också här.
lines.id: That's Oskar. He lives here too.
lines.literal: it is Oskar. he lives also here.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Why is he sitting out there?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Han dricker kaffe. Svenskar dricker mycket kaffe.
lines.id: He's having coffee. Swedes drink a lot of coffee.
lines.literal: he drinks coffee. Swedes drink much coffee.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Jo, men inte på kvällen. Då sover jag inte.
lines.id: Oh yes, I do — but not in the evening. Then I can't sleep.
lines.literal: yes-indeed, but not in evening-the. then sleep I not.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: How do you say "ngantuk" (sleepy) in Swedish?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Trött. Och det är jag nu. God natt!
lines.id: Trött. And that's what I am now. Good night!
lines.literal: tired. and that am I now. good night!

notes: **Det är** is the most useful sentence opener in all of Swedish: "it is…" / "that is…". It's used for things, people, weather and situations — *det är kallt* (it's cold), *det är bra* (that's good), *det är Oskar*. It's pronounced **deh eh**, two short sounds melting into one.

**Det här / det där** — "this one" and "that one". Swedish attaches a place word to the pointing word: *här* (here) and *där* (there) — rather like saying "this here" and "that there" in casual English. There's also a short form *detta* (this), but it smells of formal writing; in conversation people say *det här*.

**Inte always comes after the verb.** *Det är inte mjölk*, *jag talar inte svenska*, *han sover inte*. English puts "not" after a helper verb (*I do not speak*), but Swedish has no helper — so *inte* simply follows the main verb: "I speak not Swedish". If you slip and say *jag inte talar*, you'll still be understood — but it marks you instantly as a beginner. The only place *inte* moves in front of the verb is inside a subordinate clause, and that's for Unit 18.

**Jo is not ja.** When a question **contains a negative** — *Dricker du inte kaffe?* ("Don't you drink coffee?") — and your answer contradicts it, say **jo**, not *ja*. Answering *ja* there can sound as if you agree that you don't drink coffee. English muddles through with "Yes, I do!" and a firm tone; Swedish has a dedicated word (like German *doch* or French *si*), and Swedes use it dozens of times a day.

**Man** means "one" or "people" in the sense of "people in general". *Man äter det till frukost* = "people eat it for breakfast" (literally "one eats it…"). It's as common as the general "you" or "they" in everyday English — and far more common than the passive.

**Mycket** means "much / a lot of" with things you don't count (coffee, time, money) and "very" in front of adjectives: *mycket gott* (really good). For things you can count, the right word is *många*: *många böcker* (many books) — the same split as English *much* and *many*. It's pronounced **MÜK-keh** — the *c* is silent.

grammars.title: Two ways to ask a question
body: Swedish has no helper verb like English *do*. Making a question is simply a matter of moving the verb to the front — just as English does with *Are you…?* or *Can you…?*, but with every verb.
after: Notice that **the verb never leaves second place** except in yes/no questions, where it moves up to first place. The "verb in second place" rule is the backbone of Swedish word order, and all of Unit 3 is devoted to it.

Your tone of voice is **not enough** to make a question. Saying *du talar svenska?* with a rising tone can be understood — just like "You speak Swedish?" in English — but the proper way is to swap the order.

grammars.title: Seven question words
after: **Var** and **vart** are a pair that often get mixed up: *var* asks about a **location** ("where?"), *vart* asks about a **direction** ("where to?"). *Var är du?* — where are you? *Vart ska du?* — where are you going? English has mostly lost the difference (old English had *where* and *whither*), but Swedish still uses it every day.

**Hur mår du?** is the real "how are you?". The standard answers: *Bra, tack!* (fine, thanks), *Ganska bra* (pretty good), *Så där* (so-so), *Inte så bra* (not so good). Unlike English "How are you?", the question is meant seriously — Swedes actually wait for your answer.

blocks.text: Swedish has just one word for negating a sentence: **inte**. No contractions like *don't / isn't / can't*, no *do*-support, and no two-part negation like French *ne… pas*.

To negate a **noun** there's a separate word: **ingen / inget / inga**, meaning "no" or "not any". *Jag har inga pengar* (I have no money at all) sounds stronger than *jag har inte pengar* — just like English "I have no money" versus "I don't have money". The form follows the noun's gender, and that will make sense after Unit 4.

blocks.title: Ja, nej, jo
items: **Ja** — "yes" to an ordinary question. *Talar du svenska?* — *Ja.*
**Jo** — "yes, I do / yes, it is" in reply to a question that contains a negative. *Talar du inte svenska?* — *Jo, det gör jag!* ("Yes, I do!")

Picking the wrong one of *ja* and *jo* is the most common mistake foreigners make, and it can turn your answer into its opposite. If the question contains *inte*, the positive answer is almost always **jo**.

sections.title: Things in the kitchen, and a habit called fika

blocks.text: The vocabulary in this unit gathers in the kitchen on purpose, because that's where the first conversations in a Swedish student corridor nearly always happen.

**Fika** is a Swedish word with no translation. It means sitting down together, drinking coffee or tea and eating something sweet — not just a "coffee break", because what matters is the sitting together, not the coffee. It's a noun (*en fika*) and a verb (*att fika*), and it's an official part of the working day: many Swedish offices stop twice a day for it.

blocks.title: Phrases you'll use this week
items: **Ska vi fika?** — Shall we have a fika? (the most common invitation in Sweden)
**Vad heter det på svenska?** — What's that called in Swedish?
**Ursäkta?** — Sorry? (to ask someone to repeat; pronounced *ür-SHEK-tah*)
**God natt.** — Good night (when going to bed, not as a greeting).

exercises.prompt: Turn into a yes/no question by moving the verb to the front.
Negate these sentences by putting *inte* in the right place.
Fill in the right question word: *vad*, *vem*, *var*, *när*, *hur*, *varför*.
Answer with *ja*, *nej* or *jo*. (A positive answer to a negative question uses *jo*.)

answers: Bor du i Stockholm? — Dricker han kaffe? — Är det gott? — Talar ni svenska? — Kommer hon från Göteborg? — Sitter de i köket?
Jag förstår inte svenska. — Det är inte mjölk. — Han bor inte här. — Vi dricker inte kaffe på kvällen. — Du vet det inte. — Hon är inte trött.
